```{python}
import sys

from shared.components import (
    chart_card,
    method_and_sources,
    prev_next,
    related_studies,
    stat_tile,
    stat_tiles,
)
from shared.glossary import glossary_popovers
from shared.outputs import read_output
from shared.paths import CASE_STUDIES, REPO_URL, ROOT

STUDY = CASE_STUDIES / "09_retail_prices"
sys.path.insert(0, str(STUDY / "analysis"))
import figures as F  # noqa: E402

food, prov_food, notes_food = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "food_prices.csv")
fc, prov_fc, notes_fc = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "food_change.csv")
nonfood, prov_nf, notes_nf = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "nonfood_prices.csv")
nc, prov_nc, notes_nc = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "nonfood_change.csv")
check, prov_check, notes_check = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "retail_crosscheck.csv")

F0, F1 = 2013, int(food.year.max())  # food base agreed 19 Oct 2026 (2010–2012 repeat)
N0, N1 = int(nonfood.year.min()), int(nonfood.year.max())
FLAT = 0.5  # % either way counted as "little change", as in the chart legend


def pct(v):
    return F.signed(v)


def money(v):
    return F.money(v)


f = fc.set_index("label")
n = nc.set_index("label")
rose, fell = int((fc.change_pct >= FLAT).sum()), int((fc.change_pct <= -FLAT).sum())
flat = len(fc) - rose - fell
top, bottom = f.change_pct.idxmax(), f.change_pct.idxmin()
by_group = fc.groupby("group").change_pct
fish = fc[fc.group == "Fish and prawns"]
dairy = fc[fc.group == "Milk, eggs and fats"]
dairy_up = dairy[dairy.change_pct >= FLAT]
unchanged = nc[nc.change_pct.abs() < 0.05]
set_unchanged = unchanged[unchanged.set_price]
moved = nc[nc.change_pct.abs() >= 0.05]
repeat = int(food[food.year == F0].repeated_2010_2012.sum())
d = food[food.year.between(F0, F1)]
span = d.groupby("label").index_2013.agg(["min", "max"])
span["width"] = span["max"] - span["min"]
widest = span.width.sort_values(ascending=False).index[:2].tolist()
within_10 = ((span["min"] >= 90) & (span["max"] <= 110)).sum()

# Stated in the text below; stop the build rather than publish them if the data changes.
assert (len(fc), rose, fell, flat) == (24, 13, 9, 2)
assert top == "Shallot" and bottom == "Chicken eggs"
assert (fish.change_pct > -FLAT).all() and (fish.change_pct >= 5).sum() == 5
assert len(dairy) - len(dairy_up) == 4 and dairy_up.label.tolist() == ["Butter"]
assert len(nc) == 11 and len(unchanged) == 10 and len(set_unchanged) == 10
assert moved.label.tolist() == ["Cement"] and not moved.set_price.any()
assert widest == ["Garlic", "Shallot"] and span.loc["Garlic", "max"] > 130
assert within_10 > len(fc) / 2  # "most items stay within 10 points" (chart 2 alt text)
assert repeat == 18 and check.differences.iloc[1:].sum() == 0
assert check.max_difference_bnd.max() <= 0.05
```

::: {.study-intro}
This case study looks at the **[average retail prices]{.term term="average-retail-price"} of
selected everyday items** published on data.gov.bn, item by item: 24 food items in five groups
from `{python} F0` to `{python} F1`, and 11 non-food items, most of them
[Government-set prices]{.term term="set-price"}, from `{python} N0` to `{python} N1`. Prices
are in Brunei dollars, as published. It shows **what changed, not why**.

It asks two questions, answered in the conclusion:

1. **Which food items cost more in `{python} F1` than in `{python} F0`, and which cost less?**
2. **Did the non-food prices change from `{python} N0` to `{python} N1`?**
:::

```{python}
stat_tiles(
    stat_tile(f"Food items that cost more, {F1}", f"{rose} of {len(fc)}", "", f"than in {F0} ({fell} cost less)"),
    stat_tile(f"Largest rise, {F0}–{F1}", pct(f.loc[top, "change_pct"]), "", f"{top.lower()}s, per kg"),
    stat_tile(f"Non-food prices unchanged, {N0}–{N1}", f"{len(unchanged)} of {len(nc)}", "", "all of them Government-set"),
)
```

## Food prices, 2013–2018

The food table groups its items the way the price list is published: rice and cereals, meat,
milk, eggs and fats, fish and prawns, and vegetables and fruits. The tree below keeps that
grouping and gives every item the same row, because prices per kilogramme, per tin and per
tray can't be added together.

**`{python} rose` of the `{python} len(fc)` items cost more in `{python} F1` than in
`{python} F0`**, `{python} fell` cost less and `{python} flat` changed by under
`{python} f"{FLAT}%"`. Shallots rose the most (`{python} pct(f.loc["Shallot", "change_pct"])`,
from `{python} money(f.loc["Shallot", "price_2013"])` to
`{python} money(f.loc["Shallot", "price_2018"])` per kg). Chicken eggs fell the most
(`{python} pct(f.loc["Chicken eggs", "change_pct"])` a tray).

```{python}
fig, table = F.food_tree(fc, F0, F1)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title=f"{rose} of {len(fc)} food items cost more in {F1} than in {F0}; shallots rose the most",
    subtitle=f"Change in average retail price by item, grouped as published, % · {F0} to {F1}",
    alt=(
        f"A tree of five food groups and their {len(fc)} items, each with its price change. "
        f"Largest rises: shallot {pct(f.loc['Shallot', 'change_pct'])}, butter "
        f"{pct(f.loc['Butter', 'change_pct'])}, watermelon {pct(f.loc['Watermelon', 'change_pct'])}. "
        f"Largest falls: chicken eggs {pct(f.loc['Chicken eggs', 'change_pct'])}, papaya "
        f"{pct(f.loc['Papaya', 'change_pct'])}, garlic {pct(f.loc['Garlic', 'change_pct'])}. "
        f"Every fish and prawn item rose or stayed level."
    ),
    provenance=prov_fc,
    table=table,
    mobile_fig=F.food_tree(fc, F0, F1, compact=True)[0],
)
```

Within the groups, the picture differs. **Every fish and prawn item cost more or about the
same**: five of the six rose by 5% or more, led by salted anchovies
(`{python} pct(f.loc["Salted anchovies", "change_pct"])`). In milk, eggs and fats, four of the
five items cost less, and butter rose (`{python} pct(f.loc["Butter", "change_pct"])`). Meat
changed little apart from beef (`{python} pct(f.loc["Beef", "change_pct"])`).

### Start and end years don't show the swings

Comparing two years hides what happened in between. Garlic, for example, was
`{python} f"{span.loc['Garlic', 'min']:.0f}"` in its lowest year and
`{python} f"{span.loc['Garlic', 'max']:.0f}"` in its highest (`{python} F0` = 100), then ended
at `{python} f"{d[(d.label == 'Garlic') & (d.year == F1)].index_2013.iloc[0]:.0f}"`. The chart
shows each item's lowest-to-highest range from `{python} F0` to `{python} F1`, with a dot for
`{python} F1`.

```{python}
fig, table = F.food_ranges(food, F0, F1, widest)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title=f"Garlic and shallot prices swung the most between {F0} and {F1}",
    subtitle=f"Lowest to highest yearly price, index ({F0} = 100), and the {F1} value (dot) · {F0}–{F1}",
    alt=(
        f"Range bars for {len(fc)} food items. Garlic ranges from "
        f"{span.loc['Garlic', 'min']:.0f} to {span.loc['Garlic', 'max']:.0f} and shallot from "
        f"{span.loc['Shallot', 'min']:.0f} to {span.loc['Shallot', 'max']:.0f}; most items stay "
        f"within 10 points of {F0}."
    ),
    provenance=prov_food,
    table=table,
    height=620,
)
```

## Non-food prices, 2015–2025

The non-food table lists 11 items. Ten of them are **[Government-set prices]{.term
term="set-price"}**: water and electricity charged in bands, piped and cylinder gas, and two
passport fees. **All ten were the same in `{python} N1` as in `{python} N0`.** The only item
whose price changed was cement, a shop price, from
`{python} money(n.loc["Cement", "price_2015"])` to
`{python} money(n.loc["Cement", "price_2025"])` a 10 kg bag
(`{python} pct(n.loc["Cement", "change_pct"])`).

```{python}
fig, table = F.nonfood_tree(nc, N0, N1)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title=f"{len(set_unchanged)} of {len(nc)} non-food prices were the same in {N1} as in {N0}; only cement changed",
    subtitle=f"Change in price by item, grouped as published, % · {N0} to {N1}",
    alt=(
        f"A tree of two groups and {len(nc)} items. Water, electricity, piped gas, cylinder gas "
        f"and both passport fees show no change. Cement fell {abs(n.loc['Cement', 'change_pct']):.1f}%."
    ),
    provenance=prov_nc,
    table=table,
    mobile_fig=F.nonfood_tree(nc, N0, N1, compact=True)[0],
)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="About the Government-set prices"}
- **Which items.** Water supply, prepaid electricity, piped gas, cylinder gas (LPG) and the
  International and Borneo passports. The table doesn't label them; this page marks them as
  set prices because they are tariffs and fees rather than shop prices.
- **Bands.** Water and electricity are each listed in bands of use, with a price per unit or
  per kWh for each band. The table doesn't say what a water "unit" is, and gives no unit for
  piped or cylinder gas.
- **What the data shows.** Each price was the same in every year from `{python} N0` to the
  latest, `{python} N1`. The data doesn't say how these prices are set or when they last
  changed.
:::

## Conclusion

- **Which food items cost more in `{python} F1` than in `{python} F0`, and which cost less?**
  `{python} rose` of `{python} len(fc)` cost more and `{python} fell` cost less. Shallots rose
  the most (`{python} pct(f.loc["Shallot", "change_pct"])`) and chicken eggs fell the most
  (`{python} pct(f.loc["Chicken eggs", "change_pct"])`). Every fish and prawn item rose or
  stayed level, while most milk, egg and fat items cost less.
- **Did the non-food prices change from `{python} N0` to `{python} N1`?** Not the
  Government-set ones: all ten were the same in every year. Cement, the one shop price, was
  `{python} pct(n.loc["Cement", "change_pct"])` lower.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" title="Notes on the data"}
- **Why food starts in `{python} F0`.** The food table covers 2010–2018, but
  `{python} repeat` of the 24 items have exactly the same price in 2010, 2011 and 2012, often
  to several decimals. That looks like values carried forward rather than new prices, and it
  changes the results: chicken eggs were
  `{python} money(food[(food.label == "Chicken eggs") & (food.year == 2010)].price_bnd.iloc[0])`
  a tray in 2010, so from 2010 they would show a rise. All years are in the data tables.
- **Group totals left out.** The food table gives each group a value that is the sum of its
  items' prices, mixing kilogrammes, tins and trays. It has no meaning, so it isn't used. The
  table's unit header says "BND Million"; the prices are in Brunei dollars.
- **Items without prices.** Rice and bread are listed with "-" in every year, and the "Milk,
  Egg and Oil" group lists no oils. Cooking oils and rice are in the subsidised items table
  used in case study 01.
- **2013 listed twice.** The food file lists 2013 twice; the two lists differ only for salted
  anchovies (B$11.81 and B$11.80). This page uses B$11.80, which matches the older
  "Continued" edition.
:::

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" title="What this doesn't tell us"}
- **Why prices changed.** The data shows how much prices moved, not what moved them.
- **How the averages were made.** The tables don't say how many shops, brands or months each
  average covers, or whether the items stayed exactly the same over the years.
- **The cost of living.** These are single items, not a weighted basket. For prices overall,
  see the consumer price index in case study 01.
- **Food after `{python} F1`.** The latest food table ends in `{python} F1`.
:::
